implementation_notes: The standard delegate library supplies the forwarding half: subclass SimpleDelegator (or Delegator) and it sends unknown methods through method_missing to the object returned by __getobj__, so the forwarder is a small subclass and the revocation check is one guard inside method_missing. Because the guard and the delegate call happen in the same method_missing invocation, revocation is atomic per call and no flag is read across a boundary. The same file documents DelegateClass for the class-inheritance form and Forwardable for explicit per-method delegation when full control is not needed.
code_sketch:
require "delegate"
class SessionFwd < SimpleDelegator
  def initialize(target)
    super
    @revoked = false
  end
  def method_missing(name, *args, &blk)
    raise CapabilityRevoked, name.to_s if @revoked
    super
  end
  def revoke = @revoked = true        # only the grantor keeps this handle
end
pitfalls: Methods that Delegator implements itself (==, eql?, !, freeze, marshal_dump) do not pass through method_missing, so they keep working after revocation and can still reveal the delegate; override them if that matters.
The guard must come before super in method_missing; a proxy that revokes by swapping __getobj__ to nil turns the next call into a NoMethodError on nil instead of a deliberate revocation error.

Nothing stops the collaborator from calling __getobj__ or instance_variable_get, which hands back the target: treat the wrapper as in-process discipline, not as a security boundary, unless the target is truly unreachable.

variants.name: BasicObject forwarder with an explicit method_missing
variants.implementation_notes: For a forwarder that should expose nothing beyond the target, subclass BasicObject - the documented root for object hierarchies independent of Object and Kernel, and the same base Delegator uses - and implement method_missing plus respond_to_missing?. Delegation is then fully explicit and the wrapper has no inherited method surface that can bypass the guard, at the cost of re-implementing conveniences such as equality, inspect and respond_to? by hand.
pitfalls: BasicObject has almost no methods, so diagnostics that call inspect or class on the wrapper break unless you add them; raise through ::Kernel.raise because the wrapper has no raise of its own.
Skipping respond_to_missing? makes respond_to? and duck-typing checks lie about the wrapper, which shows up as odd NoMethodError paths rather than a clear revocation failure.
